subject: Estimating abundance for loud bird species (detected most often at >90 m)

messages.author: 16d7a0e159408512
messages.subject: Estimating abundance for loud bird species (detected most often at >90 m)
parts:
Hi all, 

I am writing to inquire about a predicament I have with the species I observed most often (>1000 observations) during my three year study. Here are some details to provide context:

Study design:
I conducted point count surveys at three different treatments (bison, cattle, and ungrazed) across three different seasons (May-June 2015, 2016, 2017). I have 20 point count stations at each treatment, and visited each point count station 5 times within a season. I collected data in 5-minute intervals, and denoted the minute in which I heard or saw a bird. The covariates I collected include continous covariates (exact distances, cloud cover, vegetation height, and vegetation cover) and categorical covariates (wind, rain, observer). Each point count is spaced between 200-250 m apart, and I am truncating 10% of the largest observed distances for my analyses per recommendations in Buckland et al.'s Introduction to Distance Sampling: Estimating Abundance of Biological Populations (2001).

Analysis:
I am using program Distance to estimate abundance of bird species at each site and within each year, thus I plan to divide observations between sites (bison, cattle, ungrazed) and year (2015, 2016, and 2017). The bird species I am having trouble with is Western Meadowlarks. This is a loud bird that was most often detected around 100m or greater (see graph of detection probability attached). I have not been able to fit any models to this data. My p-value for the K-S goodness of fit test is usually around 0.003. 

My question is whether anyone has advice on how to deal with data on loud birds heard at far distances. I found a few sources on removal data with Ovenbirds, where the analyses included the number of birds seen in 4 consecutive 3-minute intervals (from a 12-minute observation period), but this data did not deal with multiple visits (source: http://abc.museucienciesjournals.cat/files/ABC-27-1-pp-375-386.pdf). The only other source I found dealt with Northern Bobwhites, which also call loudly and were detected at far distances (source: http://fwspubs.org/doi/pdf/10.3996/092010-JFWM-033?code=ufws-site). This article stated that occupancy anlayses might work better for loud birds. However, when I conducted occupancy analysis for Western Meadowlarks, occupancy was 1 across all sites. With the large number of detections for Western Meadowlarks, I feel like I should be able to conduct analyses of abundance, so any advice on how best to proceed with this would be much appreciated!

Best,
Kate

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Estimating abundance for loud bird species (detected most often at >90 m)
parts:
Kate

Thanks for sending along your detection function curve for your meadowlarks.  Is the graph you provided for all years and treatments combined?  You note that there are >1000 observations in this analysis; that amount of data will flag fairly minute discrepancies as lack of fit.  It might be more informative to have a look at the probability detection function curve produced by Distance when analysing point transect data.

However, from looking at the data you provided, it does appear that detectability is high out to 100m; perhaps a hazard rate key function (with a flatter shoulder) might be the preferable model.  It might well be the case that the small p-values are the result of rounding of distances to favoured values (100, 150, perhaps 75?).  You might bin your data for the chi-square goodness of fit test being cognisant of these favoured distances and examine the resulting GOF results to assess whether lack of fit might be a result of rounding distance measurements. 

It may be the case that taking these steps in your analysis, the goodness of fit might not be so bad.

Hi Eric,

Thanks so much for your advice! I answer your question below:

Is the graph you provided for all years and treatments combined? Yes, but I plan to separate the data by site and year. Upon exploring the data separated by site and year, the graphs look similar to the one I provided in my initial post, and I get similar model fit (poor). I will try to bin the data and look at the Hazard Rate function, as well as the probability density function.

Thanks again!

Best,
Kate
